mood: The stock fell about two-thirds in 2022. Investors were angry about billions spent on the metaverse, and the company had just cut 11,000 jobs.
otherNews: It announced a $40bn share buyback, cut its 2023 cost forecast to $89–95bn (from $94–100bn), and called 2023 its 'year of efficiency'.
why: Profit missed badly, but investors were looking ahead. Lower costs and a huge buyback meant future profits per share would rise.

mood: Its crackdown on password sharing had added millions of new subscribers, and the stock had risen sharply over the past year. Investors expected another big quarter.
otherNews: It forecast next-quarter revenue of $9.49bn, below the $9.54bn analysts expected, and said it would stop reporting subscriber numbers from 2025.
why: The quarter was great, but investors pay for future growth. A weak forecast and hiding subscriber numbers suggested the fast growth was slowing.

mood: The stock was hovering near multi-year lows heading into the print. Investors were deeply pessimistic, braced for a brutal 87% plunge in quarterly profits and an ongoing exodus of market share to fast-growing rivals.
otherNews: It warned that new tariffs could add costs of approximately $1bn.
why: The stock surged 15% in a single session after better-than-feared Q4 earnings. Investors found relief in early signs that the new CEO's plan to revive product innovation and repair wholesale relationships was taking hold.

mood: The stock had climbed about 34% since the start of August to a record high, and analysts were racing to keep up. It now traded at more than 200 times next year's expected profits, against about 35 for the biggest US tech companies.
otherNews: It forecast next-quarter revenue of just over $1.3bn, ahead of the $1.2bn analysts expected, and raised its full-year forecast to $4.4bn from $4.15bn, despite fears the US government shutdown would hurt sales.
why: The results were excellent, but at that price investors already expected excellent. A beat and a raise couldn't justify paying even more, so the stock fell.

mood: Investors were cautious, fearing weak sales of its new phone, slow uptake of its new AI features, and China headwinds before earnings.
otherNews: It forecast only 'low to mid-single digit' sales growth for the holiday quarter, and said early sales of its newest phone were stronger than last year's model.
why: Apple reported a slight earnings beat alongside conservative low-to-mid single-digit revenue growth guidance for the upcoming holiday quarter. With no dramatic operational surprises to shift sentiment, the market reacted modestly.

mood: Investors avoided the stock, which fell over 35% by mid-2024, due to severe anxiety over market share losses to competitors and massive cash burn from its costly factory expansion.
otherNews: It said it would cut more than 15% of its staff, stop paying its dividend and cut $10bn of costs. For next quarter it forecast a loss of 3 cents a share on $12.5–13.5bn of revenue, while analysts expected a 31-cent profit on $14.35bn.
why: The results missed, the forecast was far below expectations, and scrapping the dividend and cutting 15% of staff showed how deep the trouble ran. Investors were worried because it had swung to a $1.61bn loss, rivals like AMD and Qualcomm were taking market share, and its data centre sales were shrinking. There was also a lack of immediate revenue because high upfront costs failed to pay off yet.

mood: Investors were anxious, weighing legal antitrust threats, generative AI search disruption, and heavy spending, leaving the underperforming stock range-bound.
otherNews: Its cloud business grew nearly 35% to $11.35bn on demand for its AI products, overall revenue grew 15%, and its new finance chief said it would keep cutting costs.
why: Although the company comfortably beat expectations behind strong core segment growth, ongoing regulatory pressure and surging capital spending limited broader investor enthusiasm.

mood: Investors were anxious and demanding, weighed down by sky-high expectations and fears that AI spending was nearing its peak. Despite a run of good news, the stock was up only about 5% for the year.
otherNews: It forecast next-quarter revenue of $76.44–79.56bn, well above the $72.8bn analysts expected, and its gross margin rose to 75%.
why: Although the company beat estimates and raised guidance, a rally that had already priced in strong data centre demand and worries about how long AI spending could keep growing prompted profit-taking.

mood: Investors were optimistic as cost-cutting paid off and ad revenue rebounded, pushing the stock near all-time highs before earnings.
otherNews: It announced its first-ever dividend ($0.50 a share every quarter), added $50bn to its share buyback, and forecast next-quarter revenue of $34.6–37bn, above the $33.6bn analysts expected.
why: The company delivered a massive earnings blowout and initiated its first-ever dividend alongside a $50bn buyback, triggering a historic stock surge.

mood: Investors were optimistic yet demanding, driven by a strong year-to-date rally and expanding AI infrastructure partnerships alongside high valuation expectations.
otherNews: Its remaining performance obligations (contracted revenue it hasn't delivered yet) jumped 359% to $455bn, helped by four multibillion-dollar contracts. It forecast cloud infrastructure revenue of $18bn this year, rising to $144bn in four years.
why: A massive surge in remaining performance obligations and multi-billion-dollar cloud contract wins signaled overwhelming AI demand, triggering a violent upside breakout.

disguise: A big tech software and cloud company
mood: Investors were already uneasy as the stock lagged the market, harboring growing anxiety over massive capital expenditures and whether cloud revenue growth could justify the spending pace.
otherNews: It spent $37.5bn on data centres and equipment in the quarter, well above the $34.3bn expected. Its cloud business grew 39%, a little slower than the quarter before, and it forecast a slightly lower profit margin than analysts expected for next quarter.
why: Despite top and bottom-line beats, cloud revenue growth showed signs of deceleration while capital expenditure surged 66% to a record $37.5 billion, triggering fears of shrinking margins and delayed AI monetization.

disguise: A global retail and tech giant
mood: Investors were cautiously hopeful as deep workforce cuts boosted profitability, though persistent cloud growth deceleration kept enthusiasm restrained.
otherNews: Its profit jumped to $10.6bn from $278m a year earlier, ad sales beat expectations at $14.7bn, and it called the holiday season record-breaking. It forecast next-quarter revenue of $138–143.5bn, around the $142.1bn analysts expected.
why: Strong holiday sales, strong advertising growth, and massive profit margin expansion proved cost-cutting efforts paid off while cloud revenue stabilized.

mood: Investors were deeply discouraged following an underwhelming robotaxi unveiling, anxious over stagnating core sales and persistent profit margin erosion.
otherNews: Its CEO said his best guess was 20–30% vehicle growth next year, well above the roughly 15% analysts expected. Its car profit margin came in around 17%, ahead of the roughly 15% expected, though $739m of profit came from selling regulatory credits to other carmakers.
why: Although revenue missed estimates, an unexpected expansion in automotive gross margins and an aggressive forecast of up to 30% vehicle growth for the following year sparked a dramatic short squeeze.

disguise: A global digital entertainment subscription leader
mood: Investors were cautiously optimistic near record highs, eager for the final quarterly subscriber disclosure before key transparency metrics sunset.
otherNews: It added a record 19 million members, passing 300 million in total, and raised its full-year revenue forecast to $43.5–44.5bn. It also announced price rises of $1–2 a month on some plans.
why: Although massive live events and hit releases drove subscriber additions past 300 million, the initial stock surge pulled back as profit-taking set in near all-time highs.

mood: Investors were euphoric near all-time highs, driven by soaring ad revenue and growing confidence that early AI investments were actively optimizing core engagement.
otherNews: It warned of a 'significant acceleration' in infrastructure spending in 2025 as it keeps investing heavily in AI. Daily users came in at 3.29 billion, just below the 3.31 billion expected, though profit grew 35% to $15.7bn.
why: Despite surpassing revenue and profit estimates, warnings of a 'significant acceleration' in infrastructure capital expenditures for 2025 stoked fears of long-term margin erosion.

mood: Investors were cautiously optimistic yet watchful, navigating fears over rising fuel costs and capacity growth while hoping strong summer travel demand would hold.
otherNews: It announced a $1.5bn share buyback, its first since the pandemic, and forecast next-quarter earnings of $2.50–3.00 a share against the $2.68 analysts expected. Net profit was still down 15% on a year earlier.
why: Investors piled in after the carrier announced a surprise $1.5 billion share repurchase program—its first since the pandemic—alongside upbeat quarterly earnings and a strong forward profit forecast.

disguise: A fast-growing US mass-market cosmetics brand
mood: Investors were increasingly nervous as the stock slid ahead of earnings, hoping strong holiday demand would sustain its multi-year momentum despite lingering concerns over slowing category growth.
otherNews: It cut its full-year forecast after a softer-than-expected January: earnings of $3.27–3.32 a share, down from $3.47–3.53, and sales growth of 27–28%, down from 28–30%. Most of its products are made in China, where new US tariffs had just begun.
why: Despite a strong third-quarter sales beat, management slashed its full-year guidance due to a sharp drop in January consumption, while new China tariffs threatened future margins.

mood: Investors were optimistic yet cautious, riding a massive multi-year turnaround while watching whether rapid unit expansion could sustain high profit-per-vehicle margins.
otherNews: It sold a record 416,348 cars in 2024 (up 33%) and made a $159m profit in the quarter, after a $200m loss a year earlier, though profit per car sold fell from the quarter before. Its 2025 outlook promised only 'significant' growth in cars sold and profit, with no numbers.
why: Although fourth-quarter unit growth and profit numbers beat expectations, sequential margin compression and shrinking wholesale volumes triggered profit-taking after the recent stock run-up.

mood: The stock had fallen about 19% since the start of the year, well below where it traded a few months earlier. Investors wanted proof the company could grow and make money at the same time.
otherNews: Gross bookings (the total value of all rides) rose 17% to $3.7bn. Its press release first said a key profit margin would grow by 500 basis points (5 percentage points) in 2024, which sent shares soaring after hours. On the evening call it corrected the figure to 50 basis points.
why: Even after the typo was fixed, the real numbers were strong: earnings more than doubled what analysts expected and bookings beat forecasts. With expectations low after a weak start to the year, buyers kept piling in all day.
tag: A real beat, not just a typo

mood: The stock had already fallen about a third in 2025, after the company cut its sales forecast twice. Customer visits had dropped for two quarters in a row.
otherNews: It cut its full-year forecast for the third time this year: same-store sales (sales at restaurants open at least a year) are now expected to fall slightly, instead of staying flat. Customer visits fell again, and it said younger diners were coming less often.
why: A third forecast cut showed the slowdown was getting worse, not better, and the company said sales were still weakening in October. It was the stock's worst day since 2012.

mood: The stock had risen about 22% in 2025 to close to its high, as investors bet on a huge merger it had completed two months earlier.
otherNews: Including one-off costs, it made a $4.3bn loss, mostly from setting aside $8.8bn to cover possible bad loans it took on in the merger. It also said the cost of combining the two companies would be higher than planned.
why: Underlying profit easily beat forecasts, but the huge headline loss and rising merger costs left investors unsure what the combined bank would really earn. An early jump faded, and the stock ended almost flat.

mood: The company had already raised its forecast twice this year, but the stock had drifted sideways for three months heading into the all-important holiday season.
otherNews: It raised its full-year sales forecast for the third time, to growth of 1.5–2% from 'up slightly', ahead of the 0.4% analysts expected. It also said the holiday season had got off to a strong start.
why: A big profit beat and a third forecast raise right before the holidays sent the stock soaring at the open. Some of the jump faded during the day, but it still closed up 13%.

mood: The stock had risen about 12% in 2024, and investors hoped the company would raise its profit forecast after a strong start to the year.
otherNews: Higher warranty costs (repairs it pays for on cars it has already sold), mostly on 2021 and older models, cut into profit. It kept its full-year profit forecast at $10–12bn instead of raising it.
why: A big profit miss caused by repair bills on older cars showed its quality problems were still costing money, and keeping the forecast unchanged disappointed investors who had hoped for a raise. The stock slid further through the day.

mood: The stock had climbed more than 20% in three months, far ahead of other drinks companies, and was close to its highest level of the year.
otherNews: Sales fell 2.3%, which it blamed on how distributors timed their orders, a stronger dollar, bad weather and one fewer selling day. Its profit margin improved, and it said orders so far this year were up about 7% after adjusting for currency (excluding its alcohol brands).
why: Sales missed badly, but the reasons looked temporary, profit still edged past forecasts and orders for the year were rising. The stock dipped at the open, then recovered to finish slightly higher.

mood: The stock had jumped about 38% in three months to its highest level in months, as investors bet its fast growth would continue.
otherNews: It raised its full-year forecast, but the new numbers implied sales would fall next quarter for the first time in years, with thinner profit margins.
why: The beat was big, but investors had priced in even more growth, and the forecast implied next quarter's sales would shrink with thinner margins. After a 12% drop at the open, selling continued all day.

mood: The stock had risen about 28% in three months, as investors hoped it could cope with tariffs after it pulled its forecast in May because of trade uncertainty.
otherNews: Sales fell 6%, with North America down 16%, as retailers delayed orders because of tariffs and sales of its biggest doll brand slowed. It brought back a lower full-year forecast and said tariffs would cost it up to $100m before any fixes.
why: Profit beat, but falling sales and a weaker outlook showed tariffs were already hurting, as stores held back on holiday orders. The stock kept sliding all day, ending down 16%.

mood: The stock had crashed about 56% in 2024 so far, though it had bounced 13% in the two weeks before the results. Investors wanted signs it could cut costs.
otherNews: Its loss widened to $1.45bn from $1.35bn a year earlier. But it kept its target of building 57,000 vehicles this year and cut its spending plan by $550m, to $1.2bn, by building its cheaper new model at its existing factory.
why: The results were mixed: a wider loss pulled the stock down at the open, but the cost cuts and an unchanged production target meant no big surprise either way. By the close, the stock was flat.

mood: The stock had fallen about a third in 2024 as US sales slowed, but it had rallied 12% in the two weeks before the results.
otherNews: Sales grew 9%, driven by strong growth outside the US while US sales slowed. Its holiday forecast was in line with expectations, with the top of its profit range a little above what analysts expected.
why: A clean beat and a steady holiday forecast reassured investors who had sold the stock all year, and buying kept building after the open. It closed up 16%.

mood: The stock had risen 12% in 2025 and was close to its highs, as shoppers kept flocking to its stores.
otherNews: Sales at existing stores rose and membership fees grew to $1.19bn. But it said it was hard to predict the impact of tariffs, as about a third of its US sales are imported goods.
why: With the stock near its highs, even a small profit miss and uncertainty over tariffs were enough to send it lower, and selling picked up through the day.

mood: The stock had climbed about 18% in three months, recovering from a weak spring.
otherNews: Sales of its main product fell short as more patients chose traditional alternatives, and it forecast lower revenue next quarter ($965–985m). It also announced job cuts and a restructuring costing $150–170m.
why: Missing on sales and profit, cutting the outlook and announcing job cuts all at once shattered hopes of a recovery. The stock opened 30% lower and kept falling.

mood: The stock fell 15% after its last results in September, then won back about half of that. Weak US industrial demand was still the worry.
otherNews: It cut its full-year forecast: revenue now flat rather than up slightly, and EPS of $19–20 instead of $20–21. It also announced plans to spin off its freight trucking business as a separate listed company within 18 months.
why: The spin-off excited investors, and the stock opened up more than 6%. But with a revenue miss and a lower forecast also on the table, the whole gain was gone by the close.

mood: The stock had lost about 28% so far in 2025 and about 45% in a year. A new CEO had just taken over, and competition was a growing worry.
otherNews: Its forecast for the year ahead was below expectations: sales of $11.5–11.6bn against $11.67bn, and EPS of $22.50–22.90 against $23.36. It said it was being cautious because shoppers seemed uncertain.
why: The forecast disappointed, but the beat was big and the stock was already so beaten down that little needed to go right. It opened up 9% and kept climbing all day.

mood: The stock was about 16% below its high of the past year and roughly flat for 2025. Investors wanted proof that growth would pick up.
otherNews: Gross profit (revenue minus direct costs) at its consumer payments app rose 16%, slower than the 21% for the full year. It forecast at least 15% gross profit growth overall in 2025, but said the first quarter would be the low point, so the plan relied on growth picking up later.
why: It missed on both revenue and profit, and its forecast asked investors to wait for a recovery later in the year. The stock opened down about 10% and kept sliding, to close down almost 18%.

disguise: A US luxury home furnishings retailer
mood: The stock had fallen 55% in 2025, including a 40% drop after its last results in April, just as new tariffs were announced. More than 20% of its shares were sold short: bets that the price would keep falling.
otherNews: It made a surprise profit and kept its full-year forecast of 10–13% revenue growth. But it warned that tariffs would knock about 6 points off next quarter's revenue, and it delayed some product launches.
why: The surprise profit put pressure on short sellers to buy shares and close their bets, which pushed the price up further. It opened up 19%, but most of that faded and it closed up 7%.

mood: The stock had surged about 51% in three months to close to its high of the past year, as airline shares rallied on hopes that travel demand was recovering.
otherNews: It expected operating profit of at least $600m this year and said demand showed signs of improving, but next quarter's revenue per seat could be anywhere from 2% lower to 2% higher. It also announced a $2bn share buyback.
why: After such a big run, a miss and a vague outlook weren't enough, even with a buyback. It opened down less than 4%, but the selling built all day and it closed down 11%.

mood: The stock had soared about 78% in three months and was at its highest level of the past year, so expectations were sky-high.
otherNews: It raised its full-year revenue forecast to $741–744m from $731–738m, and monthly users jumped 36% to 113m. Its revenue forecast for next quarter was also above expectations.
why: Almost everything beat, but the stock had run so far that a beat was already expected, and daily users came in slightly short. It opened down 4.5%, then recovered to close down just 1%.

disguise: A global food and drink chain
mood: Nine months into a new CEO's turnaround plan, the stock was up about 11% in three months but still about 20% below its high of the past year. Same-store sales had fallen for five quarters in a row.
otherNews: Same-store sales (sales at outlets open at least a year) fell for a sixth straight quarter, but rose 2% in China. It said 11 cents of the fall in EPS came from the cost of a big staff conference.
why: One analyst called the report "less worse than expected", and the stock opened up 5%. The gain was gone by the close, and no source gives a clear reason: turnaround hopes and weak numbers simply cancelled out.

mood: The stock had fallen about 35% in a month. Two weeks earlier the company warned that medical costs were rising, cutting its full-year EPS forecast to $21.50–22.50 and pointing to about $5.50 for this quarter.
otherNews: EPS was close to what it had warned, but it cut its full-year forecast again, to at least $19. It blamed what it called a temporary gap between the premiums it charges and medical costs, which had recently risen faster.
why: A second forecast cut in about two weeks suggested costs were rising faster than the company could predict. The stock opened down 9% and kept falling, and other health insurers fell with it.

mood: The stock was already up about 25% in 2025 and close to its high of the past year.
otherNews: It blamed unusual luck: sports favourites won far more often than normal, which cost it money on customers' bets. It raised the low end of its 2025 revenue forecast to $6.3–6.6bn from $6.2–6.6bn, about 35% growth, and kept its profit forecast.
why: Investors looked past the quarter, because bad luck with sports results isn't a lasting problem and the forecast pointed to fast growth. It opened up 5% and climbed all day to close up 15%, its highest since August 2021.

mood: The stock was about 31% below its high of the past year and down 8% in three months.
otherNews: Orders for new homes fell 17%. It cut its full-year housing revenue forecast to $6.6–7bn from $7–7.5bn, below the $7.03bn analysts expected, as consumer confidence fell.
why: A miss, fewer orders and a lower forecast all pointed the same way, and the stock opened down 8%. But buyers came back during the day and it closed down 5%, so a short did best by exiting at the open.

mood: The stock had fallen about 7% in a month and was about 10% below its high of the past year.
otherNews: Total bookings rose 13% to $24.4bn, and bookings through its business-to-business arm rose 24%. It expected bookings to grow 4–6% next quarter, and said it would pay a quarterly dividend of 40 cents a share.
why: A clear beat on sales and profit, with bookings growing strongly too. It opened up 13% and kept rising all day to close up 17%.

mood: The stock had fallen about 18% in three months as the cost of cocoa soared.
otherNews: It forecast that 2025 EPS would fall about 10% because of what it called unprecedented cocoa costs, worse than the 6.7% fall analysts expected. It also forecast about 5% underlying sales growth, and said EPS should grow again in 2026.
why: It missed on revenue and profit and gave a weak forecast, and the stock opened down 3%. Then it turned around to close up 2%. No source explains why, which is a reminder that the morning's reaction isn't always the final word.

mood: The stock was up about 4% in three months and about 9% below its high of the past year. Investors were watching for signs that its slow growth could pick up.
otherNews: Its forecast for the coming year was revenue of $4.785–4.795bn, below the $4.81bn analysts expected. Its EPS forecast of $5.34–5.37 was roughly in line with the $5.36 expected.
why: It beat for the quarter, but investors cared more about what came next, and the revenue forecast fell short. It opened down 4% and kept falling to close down more than 8%.

disguise: A US oil and gas producer
mood: The stock was about 29% below its high of the past year. Investors were watching how quickly the company could pay down its debts.
otherNews: It raised its dividend 9%, finished repaying the $4.5bn of debt it had promised to, and beat its own production forecast. But including one-offs it made a loss, mainly from a $1.1bn charge after a court ruling on environmental costs.
why: Stronger profit and production, a higher dividend and a debt target met outweighed a small revenue miss and a one-off loss. It dipped after hours, opened up 1% and rose through the day to close up 4%.

mood: The stock was up about 7% in three months and about 5% below its high of the past year.
otherNews: It forecast 2025 sales growth of just 1–3% and EPS of $3.80–4.15, about 8% below expectations at the midpoint. Its sales forecast for next quarter was about 5% below expectations.
why: Sales beat, but profit missed and the forecast disappointed, so the stock opened down 8%. It recovered part of that to close down about 6%, so a short did best by exiting at the open.
